mainTopic: A sale is public while a loan is private, how this affects a buyer's year toward a חזקה, and a new משנה on who cannot make a חזקה and how one act acquires land.
overview: The amud opens by finishing רב's reasoning: later buyers who lose land have only themselves to blame, because they should have checked first. The גמרא challenges רב with a משנה that says a debt backed only by witnesses cannot be collected from sold property. It also blocks the answer that רב, as a תנא, may argue, because רב and שמואל themselves said an oral loan is not collected from heirs or buyers. The answer is that a loan is kept quiet, but a sale is made in public so that word spreads. A ברייתא then teaches that a buyer's year of use joins the father's and son's years to make a חזקה. A second ברייתא seems to show a sale is not public, since a sale by the owner's son is not counted as a מחאה. רב פפא answers that the son sold 'his fields' without naming this one. Finally, a new משנה lists people whose use cannot create a חזקה, such as craftsmen, partners, sharecroppers, guardians, spouses, and a father or son. It then teaches that for a gift, brothers dividing an inheritance, or a convert's ownerless property, one act of locking, fencing, or breaching acquires the field at once.

steps.title: The later buyers caused their own loss
steps.stepSummary: The closing words of רב's reasoning: the later buyers lose out because they should have checked first.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of רב's explanation from just before this section. The later buyers who lose their land have only themselves to blame.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ruled that a first buyer who had witnesses can take land back from later buyers if his field is seized. The reason is that the first sale was known, so later buyers should have found out about it before buying. Their loss comes from their own carelessness.

keyTerms.meaning: they caused a loss
to themselves

phrases.english: They caused their own loss.
phrases.notes: 'They' are the later buyers. They should have checked whether the land was already tied to an earlier deal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב's ruling, which began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Later buyers lose the land, because they failed to look into the earlier public sale.

steps.title: A משנה seems to contradict רב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רב really said this, since a משנה rules that a debt with only witnesses is collected only from unsold property.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רב really say this? But we learned in a משנה: one who lends with a document collects from sold, mortgaged property. One who lends with only witnesses collects only from property the borrower still owns.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב's ruling with a משנה. The משנה says that without a written document, you cannot take back property that was already sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the משנה, witnesses alone do not create a claim strong enough to take land away from buyers. רב let a buyer with only witnesses take land from later buyers. That looks like the very thing the משנה forbids.

keyTerms.meaning: and did he really say? (opens a challenge)
property tied to a debt that has since been sold to others
'free' property the borrower still owns

phrases.english: And did Rav say this?

steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that a buyer with only witnesses can collect from sold property
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה says a claim backed only by witnesses cannot reach sold property, and רב says it can.

steps.title: רב cannot simply argue, since he agrees with the rule himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא blocks the answer that רב, as a תנא, may disagree with a משנה. רב himself, together with שמואל, said an oral loan cannot be collected from heirs or buyers.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say רב has the status of a תנא and may disagree, didn't רב and שמואל both say: an oral loan is not collected from the heirs or from the buyers!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shuts down an easy escape before anyone uses it. רב usually may argue on a משנה, but here his own words agree with that משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב has a special standing that lets him disagree with a משנה. That does not help here, because רב himself ruled with שמואל that a loan without a document cannot be collected from buyers. So רב seems to contradict himself.

steps.confusionAlert: 'Oral loan' does not mean there were no witnesses. It means there was no written document, even if witnesses were present.

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב's own ruling agrees with the משנה, so his ruling about the sale seems to contradict him.

steps.title: A loan is private, but a sale is public
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a loan and a sale cannot be compared. Borrowers keep loans quiet, but sellers make sales public, so later buyers should know about an earlier sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are you comparing a loan to a sale? When someone borrows, he borrows quietly, so his property will not lose value. But someone who sells land sells it in public, so word of it will spread.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב by showing the two cases are different. A loan is hidden, but a sale is known to everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Buyers cannot be blamed for missing a loan that was kept secret, so an oral loan cannot be collected from them. A sale is made in public, so later buyers should have known about it. That is why they 'caused their own loss,' and רב's ruling stands.

keyTerms.meaning: you are raising a contradiction
a sale
quietly, in private
in public
word or news that spreads
become cheap, lose value

steps.whatToRemember: A loan is kept private, so buyers are not blamed for not knowing about it. A sale is public, so buyers are expected to know about it. That is why רב lets a sale made with only witnesses reach later buyers.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that collecting from buyers depends on whether they could have known about the earlier claim.

A loan: when one borrows,

phrases.english: so that his property will not become cheap on him.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the cases: a loan is not like a sale.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought a loan with witnesses and a sale with witnesses follow the same rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: A loan is private, so buyers are not responsible for it. A sale is public, so buyers who ignore it caused their own loss.

steps.title: A buyer's year joins the earlier years to make a חזקה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that years of use by a father, then his son, then a buyer from the son, are added together to make the three years needed for a חזקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: if the father used the field one year and the son two, or the father two and the son one, or the father one, the son one and the buyer one, this is a חזקה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about the person holding the field: years used by a father, his heir, and a buyer from that heir all count together toward the three years of חזקה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father-and-son cases are simple, because an heir steps into his father's place. The new point is the buyer: his year also counts. The גמרא will read this as showing that a sale is public, so the original owner should have heard about it and protested.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'ate it'; used the field and took its produce
Presumed ownership, gained by using land openly for three years
A buyer

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
If the father used it one year and the son two years;
phrases.notes: 'Ate it' means he worked the field and took its crops. The father and son here are the ones holding the field.

phrases.english: or the father two years and the son one year;
or the father one year, and the son one year,

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֲכָלָהּ הָאָב שָׁנָה וְהַבֵּן שְׁתַּיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that fits step 4's idea that sales are public.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Years of use by father, son, and a buyer from the son combine to make a חזקה.

steps.title: Clash with a ברייתא where the owner's son sells the field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a sale really is public, since another ברייתא counts a year of use in front of the original owner's buyer. If sales were public, the owner's son selling the field would be the biggest protest of all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean a buyer has publicity? But contrast it: if he used it in front of the father one year and the son two, or the father two and the son one, or the father one, the son one and the buyer one, it is a חזקה. If you think a buyer has publicity, there is no greater protest than this!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the first ברייתא to mean that a sale is public, then challenges this with a second ברייתא, now told from the side of the original owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the second ברייתא, the original owner's son sold the field to a buyer while someone else was using it, and that year still counts toward the user's חזקה. If a sale is public, then selling the field openly should be a loud מחאה, a way of saying 'this is mine.' A מחאה should stop the חזקה, yet the ברייתא says the חזקה stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this to say...? It introduces a surprising conclusion that is about to be challenged
A 'voice'; publicity, news that spreads

A protest by the owner that stops a חזקה

steps.confusionAlert: Both ברייתות have a father, a son, and a buyer, but they are different people. In the first, they are the ones holding the field. In the second, they are the original owners, and someone else is using the field in front of them.

phrases.english: Is this to say that a buyer has publicity?!
And contrast it with this:
If he used it in the presence of the father one year
phrases.notes: Here the father, the son, and later the buyer are the original owners, watching someone else use the field.

phrases.english: and in the presence of the son two years;

phrases.english: or in the presence of the father one year, and in the presence of the son one year,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from step 5 and challenges it with a contradicting ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that a sale is public (from steps 4-5).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a sale is public, the original owner's son selling the field would be a clear מחאה and should stop the חזקה. The second ברייתא still counts that year, so it seems a sale is not public.

steps.title: רב פפא: the seller did not name this field
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the second ברייתא is about a seller who sold 'his fields' in general without naming this particular field.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: that ברייתא is talking about someone who sells his fields without saying which ones.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא settles the clash by narrowing the case of the second ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sale is public, but only what was clearly sold becomes known. When the owner's son sells 'my fields' without naming this one, the person using it has no reason to think his field is included, so the sale is not a מחאה against him. If the son had named this field, the sale would count as a מחאה.

keyTerms.meaning: When it was taught; limits a ברייתא to a specific case
His fields
Without saying which ones; in general terms

steps.whatToRemember: A sale is public, so a buyer's year can join earlier years for a חזקה. A sale by the original owner counts as a מחאה only if he clearly named the field.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
When that one was taught,
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the second ברייתא, where the owner's son sold the field.

phrases.english: it was about one who sells his fields without specifying.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כִּי תַּנְיָא הָהִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case of the contradicting source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner's son sold this field outright, so a public sale should have been a מחאה.
steps.terutzMaskana: He sold his fields in general without naming this one, so the user did not know to protest, and the חזקה stands.

steps.title: New משנה: people who cannot make a חזקה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists people whose use of property does not count as a חזקה: craftsmen, partners, sharecroppers, guardians, a husband or wife in the other's property, and a father or son in the other's property.
steps.simpleTranslation: Craftsmen, partners, sharecroppers, and guardians have no חזקה. A man has no חזקה in his wife's property, and a woman has none in her husband's. A father has none in his son's property, and a son has none in his father's.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins and lists people whose use of someone else's property does not create a חזקה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each person on the list has an ordinary reason to be holding or using the property without owning it, such as fixing it, sharing it, working it, or managing it. Close family members also use each other's things freely. So their use does not show ownership, and it cannot build a חזקה.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
Craftsmen holding items they are repairing

Guardians or managers of someone else's property
The property of

A man has no חזקה in his wife's property,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: People with an ordinary reason to hold or use someone's property, including close family, cannot gain a חזקה through that use.

steps.title: Three years is only for proof, and one act is enough to acquire
steps.stepSummary: The משנה limits the three-year rule to a person who uses a field as proof of ownership. For a gift, brothers dividing an inheritance, or a convert's property, one small act of ownership acquires the field right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: When does all of this apply? When someone uses a field to prove he already owns it. But if someone is given a field as a gift, or brothers divide an inheritance, or someone takes a convert's property, then as soon as he locks it, fences it, or breaks through its fence even a little, that counts as taking possession.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה closes its discussion by saying which cases all the earlier rules apply to. It then shows a different kind of case, where one quick act of ownership is enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The three years of use, and the people whose use does not count, belong to proving that a field already belongs to you. When a person is acquiring a field now, through a gift, an inheritance split, or a convert's ownerless property, he does not need years of use. One act that shows ownership, such as locking, fencing, or breaking the fence, acquires it on the spot.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case are these words said? A standard way of limiting a rule to certain cases.
Someone who has been using a field and claims it as his.
The property of a convert. It becomes ownerless if he dies without heirs.
He locked the door of the property.
He fenced it in.
He broke through its fence, even a little.

steps.whatToRemember: The word חזקה has two jobs. In most of this פרק it means three years of use that serve as proof of ownership. Here it means one quick act that actually acquires the field.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two kinds of חזקה. The three years are needed only to prove an old ownership claim. Locking, fencing, or breaking a fence is the way to acquire a field right now, and it works immediately.
steps.whyThisMatters: This line separates proof of ownership from acquiring ownership. That distinction comes up again and again in the laws of land.

phrases.english: In what case are these words said?
In the case of one who holds on to a field as a claim.
But in the case of one who gives a gift,
and brothers who divided an inheritance,
and one who takes hold of a convert's property:
phrases.notes: This is a convert who died with no heirs, so his property has no owner and anyone can take it.

phrases.english: if he locked, or fenced, or broke through even a little,
this is taking possession.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the earlier rules of the משנה, including the list in step 8, to proof-type חזקה. It then gives the separate rule for acquiring a field through one act.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three years of use, and the people excluded from it, apply only to someone using a field as proof of ownership. For a gift, brothers dividing an inheritance, or a convert's ownerless property, one act of locking, fencing, or breaching the fence even slightly acquires the field immediately.
